P.title: P.blurb
Money: How money works, budgeting, compound interest and investing basics.

P.title: mo-basics.summary
Money: What money is and where it comes from.

P.title: mo-basics.q0.q
Money: Roughly how long does it take for prices to double at 2% inflation?

P.title: mo-basics.q1.q
Money: What gives euro notes their value today?

P.title: mo-basics.q2.q
Money: Most money in the economy exists as…

P.title: mo-basics.c0.text
Money: Money has three jobs: a medium of exchange (you can buy with it), a unit of account (prices are measured in it) and a store of value (it keeps worth over time).

P.title: mo-basics.c1.text
Money: Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: you must find someone who has what you want and wants what you have. Money solved that.

P.title: mo-basics.c2.text
Money: Euro notes aren't backed by gold. Their value comes from trust and from law: governments accept them for taxes and require them to be accepted for debts.

P.title: mo-basics.c3.text
Money: Physical notes and coins are a small part of the money supply. Most money exists as numbers in bank accounts, created when banks lend.

P.title: mo-basics.c4.text
Money: The European Central Bank sets interest rates for the euro area, aiming for inflation close to 2% a year. Banco de Portugal is part of this system.

P.title: mo-basics.c5.text
Money: Inflation means prices rise over time, so each euro buys less. At 2% a year, prices double in about 35 years.

P.title: mo-basics.c5.viz.unit
Money: price of a basket, € (2% a year)

P.title: mo-basics.c6.text
Money: Divide 72 by an annual percentage rate to estimate how many years it takes for something to double. It works for prices, savings and debts.

P.title: mo-basics.c7.text
Money: Interest is the price of money. Borrowers pay it; savers earn it. Higher central bank rates usually mean pricier loans and better savings rates.

P.title: mo-basics.c8.text
Money: Prices rise when many people want something scarce, and fall when it's plentiful or unwanted. Concert tickets and summer flights are classic examples.

P.title: mo-basics.c9.text
Money: €10,000 kept under the mattress for 10 years with 3% inflation would buy what about €7,400 buys today.

P.title: mo-budget.q0.q
Money: How big should an emergency fund usually be?

P.title: mo-budget.c0.text
Money: Move savings out as soon as your salary arrives, not with what's left at the end of the month; there's rarely anything left.

P.title: mo-budget.c1.text
Money: A simple starting split of take-home pay: 50% on needs, 30% on wants and 20% on savings or paying off debt. Adjust to your situation.

P.title: mo-budget.c2.text
Money: Needs are things you must pay for (rent, food, transport, bills). Wants make life nicer but are optional. Many things have a need part and a want part.

P.title: mo-budget.c2.viz.items.3.b
Money: need, but the latest model is a want

P.title: mo-budget.c3.text
Money: Keep three to six months of essential expenses in an easy-access savings account. It turns a crisis, like losing a job or a broken car, into an inconvenience.

P.title: mo-budget.c4.text
Money: Most people underestimate small, frequent spending. Track every expense for one month before making a budget; the results usually surprise.

P.title: mo-budget.c5.text
Money: Streaming, apps, gym and cloud storage: €8 here, €12 there, and you may be paying for things you don't use. Check bank statements and cancel what you've forgotten.

P.title: mo-budget.c6.text
Money: Small daily savings add up, but big decisions, such as rent, car and housing, matter more. Optimise the big three before agonising over a coffee.

P.title: mo-budget.c7.text
Money: We treat money differently depending on where it came from: a tax refund feels like "free money" and gets spent. A euro is a euro wherever it comes from.

P.title: mo-budget.c7.viz.items.0.w
Money: It's a bonus, so I can blow it

P.title: mo-budget.c7.viz.items.0.r
Money: A euro is a euro: does this fit my plan?

P.title: mo-budget.c8.text
Money: When pay rises, spending tends to rise to match it. Saving half of every raise keeps your lifestyle growing while your savings grow faster.

P.title: mo-budget.c9.text
Money: Take-home pay €1,600. Needs €800, wants €480, savings €320. After six months, €1,920 saved: a start on an emergency fund.

P.title: mo-compound.q0.q
Money: What makes compound interest different from simple interest?

P.title: mo-compound.q0.o1
Money: It earns interest on past interest

P.title: mo-compound.q1.q
Money: Using the rule of 72, how long does money take to double at 6%?

P.title: mo-compound.c0.text
Money: Simple interest pays only on what you put in. Compound interest also pays on past interest, so growth speeds up over time.

P.title: mo-compound.c1.text
Money: After n years, money grows by the factor (1 + r) for each year. Small differences in r or n make huge differences.

P.title: mo-compound.c2.text
Money: After 10 years: €1,629. After 20: €2,653. After 40: €7,040. Most of the growth comes late.

P.title: mo-compound.c3.text
Money: Starting early matters more than investing a lot. Someone who invests from 25 to 35 and stops can end up with more than someone who invests from 35 to 65, at the same return.

P.title: mo-compound.c4.text
Money: Compounding works against you on debt. Credit card balances can charge 15–20% a year or more, doubling in about four or five years if unpaid.

P.title: mo-compound.c5.text
Money: A 1% yearly fee sounds tiny but compounds too. Over 30 years it can eat about a quarter of your final pot.

P.title: mo-compound.c6.text
Money: A 5% return with 3% inflation is only about 2% of real growth in buying power. Always compare returns with inflation.

P.title: mo-compound.c7.text
Money: Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world is often credited to Einstein, but there's no evidence he said it. The maths is real either way.

P.title: mo-compound.c7.viz.items.0.w
Money: Einstein called it the eighth wonder

P.title: mo-compound.c7.viz.items.0.r
Money: No evidence he ever said it

P.title: mo-compound.c8.text
Money: Adding a fixed amount every month, rather than one lump, smooths the ups and downs of markets. It's called euro-cost averaging.

P.title: mo-compound.c8.viz.steps.1
Money: Buys more when prices are low

P.title: mo-compound.c9.text
Money: Investing €100 a month at 5% a year for 30 years: you pay in €36,000, and it grows to about €83,000.

P.title: mo-invest.q1.o1
Money: To reduce the damage of any single failure

P.title: mo-invest.q1.x
Money: Don't put all eggs in one basket.

P.title: mo-invest.c0.text
Money: Saving keeps money safe for the short term. Investing buys assets that can grow over the long term, with the risk of falling in value along the way.

P.title: mo-invest.c1.text
Money: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company. You can gain if its price rises and if it pays dividends, and you can lose if it falls.

P.title: mo-invest.c2.text
Money: A bond is a loan to a government or company. They pay you interest and return the money at the end. Usually steadier than shares, with lower long-term returns.

P.title: mo-invest.c3.text
Money: Higher expected returns come with bigger swings. There's no reliable way to get high returns without accepting risk.

P.title: mo-invest.c4.text
Money: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. Spreading money across many companies, countries and asset types reduces the damage any single failure can do.

P.title: mo-invest.c5.text
Money: An index fund buys every company in an index, like the S&P 500 or a world index, at very low cost. Most actively managed funds fail to beat their index over long periods.

P.title: mo-invest.c6.text
Money: Markets fall often, sometimes sharply, but have historically recovered and grown over long periods. Missing just the best few days can badly hurt returns.

P.title: mo-invest.c6.viz.items.0.w
Money: I'll wait for the perfect moment

P.title: mo-invest.c6.viz.items.0.r
Money: Time in the market beats timing the market

P.title: mo-invest.c7.text
Money: Promises of high guaranteed returns are a red flag. If it's guaranteed, it's low; if it's high, it isn't guaranteed. Scams often push urgency and secrecy.

P.title: mo-invest.c8.text
Money: Fear makes people sell after crashes and greed makes them buy at peaks: the opposite of "buy low, sell high". A written plan helps you stick to your course.

P.title: mo-invest.c9.text
Money: A common order: clear expensive debt, build an emergency fund, then invest money you won't need for at least five years. This is general information, not personal advice.

P.title: mo-econ.q0.o1
Money: What you give up to get something

P.title: mo-econ.q1.q
Money: If inflation falls from 5% to 2%, prices…

P.title: mo-econ.c0.text
Money: Gross domestic product is the total value of goods and services a country produces in a year. It measures the size of an economy, not its wellbeing.

P.title: mo-econ.c1.text
Money: A recession is a significant fall in economic activity, often defined as two quarters in a row of falling GDP. Jobs and incomes usually suffer.

P.title: mo-econ.c2.text
Money: The real cost of something is what you give up to get it. An evening studying costs the evening out you didn't have.

P.title: mo-econ.c3.text
Money: People respond to incentives. Taxes on sugary drinks reduce sales; deposits on bottles increase recycling. Badly designed ones backfire.

P.title: mo-econ.c4.text
Money: Countries gain by specialising in what they're relatively best at and trading, even if one is better at everything. Portugal and England's wine and cloth was Ricardo's 1817 example.

P.title: mo-econ.c5.text
Money: When a shared resource is free for all, everyone overuses it. Overfishing is a classic example; quotas and ownership rules can help.

P.title: mo-econ.c6.text
Money: Taxes fund public services. Portugal uses income tax (IRS) with rates that rise with income, VAT (IVA) on purchases at 23% standard in the mainland, and social security contributions.

P.title: mo-econ.c7.text
Money: Some unemployment is normal as people change jobs. The rate is the share of people who want work and are looking for it but don't have it.

P.title: mo-econ.c8.text
Money: Exchange rates are the price of one currency in another. A stronger euro makes holidays abroad cheaper but Portuguese exports pricier for foreigners.

P.title: mo-econ.c9.text
Money: Inflation falls to 2% doesn't mean prices fell; it means they are rising more slowly. Only negative inflation, called deflation, means prices fall.

P.title: mo-econ.c9.viz.items.0.w
Money: Inflation fell, so prices are lower

P.title: mo-econ.c9.viz.items.0.r
Money: Prices still rose, just more slowly

P.title: mo-debt.q0.o1
Money: Interest plus most fees, as a yearly rate

P.title: mo-debt.q0.x
Money: The fair way to compare loans.

P.title: mo-debt.q1.q
Money: Which debt-repayment method saves the most interest?

P.title: mo-debt.q2.q
Money: Stretching a loan from 5 to 10 years usually…

P.title: mo-debt.q2.o1
Money: lowers monthly payments but costs more in total

P.title: mo-debt.c0.text
Money: Debt can be useful when it buys something that lasts or grows in value, like a home or education. Expensive debt for things that lose value quickly is riskier.

P.title: mo-debt.c1.text
Money: Compare loans by APR (TAEG in Portugal), which includes interest and most fees as a yearly rate. The lowest monthly payment isn't always the cheapest loan.

P.title: mo-debt.c2.text
Money: Stretching a loan over more years lowers the monthly payment but raises the total paid. A €10,000 loan at 8% costs about €2,170 interest over 5 years, but €4,560 over 10.

P.title: mo-debt.c3.text
Money: Paying only the minimum on a credit card can take many years and cost far more than the original purchase. Interest keeps compounding on the balance.

P.title: mo-debt.c4.text
Money: Two ways to clear several debts: the snowball pays the smallest balance first for quick wins; the avalanche pays the highest rate first and saves the most money.

P.title: mo-debt.c5.text
Money: Lenders check your record of past loans and repayments. In Portugal, the Banco de Portugal's credit register shows your responsibilities to banks.

P.title: mo-debt.c5.viz.items.2
Money: Don't apply for many loans at once

P.title: mo-debt.c6.text
Money: Lenders look at what share of your income goes on debt payments. Banco de Portugal recommends banks generally keep it at or below 50% for new loans.

P.title: mo-debt.c7.text
Money: Splitting payments into instalments feels painless, but it makes spending easier and can lead to stacked obligations and late fees.

P.title: mo-debt.c8.text
Money: Being a guarantor (fiador) means you're liable if the borrower can't pay. Only guarantee what you could afford to pay yourself.

P.title: mo-debt.c8.viz.items.0.r
Money: You may have to pay the whole debt

P.title: mo-debt.c9.text
Money: €3,000 on a card at 18% APR. Paying €100 a month takes about 40 months and ~€1,000 interest. Paying €200 cuts it to about 17 months and ~€420.

P.title: mo-banks.q0.q
Money: How much is guaranteed per depositor per bank in the EU?

P.title: mo-banks.q0.x
Money: Fundo de Garantia de Depósitos in Portugal.

P.title: mo-banks.c0.text
Money: Banks take deposits and lend most of that money out at higher rates. The difference, the interest margin, is a key source of profit.

P.title: mo-banks.c1.text
Money: When a bank makes a loan, it creates a new deposit in the borrower's account. Most money in the economy is created this way, limited by regulation and demand.

P.title: mo-banks.c2.text
Money: Banks keep only a fraction of deposits as cash and reserves. That's fine normally, but if everyone withdraws at once, a bank run can sink it.

P.title: mo-banks.c3.text
Money: In the EU, deposits are guaranteed up to €100,000 per depositor, per bank. In Portugal, this is the Fundo de Garantia de Depósitos.

P.title: mo-banks.c4.text
Money: In 2023, Silicon Valley Bank collapsed after depositors withdrew $42 billion in a single day, spurred by social media. Speed of digital runs is new.

P.title: mo-banks.c4.viz.steps.2
Money: Bank sells assets at a loss

P.title: mo-banks.c5.text
Money: After the 2008 crisis, regulators required banks to hold more of their own capital to absorb losses, so taxpayers don't have to.

P.title: mo-banks.c5.viz.items.0
Money: Bank's own capital: absorbs losses first

P.title: mo-banks.c6.text
Money: Banks also earn from fees: account maintenance, transfers, cards. Comparing fees can save tens of euros a year; Banco de Portugal publishes comparisons.

P.title: mo-banks.c7.text
Money: Most Portuguese mortgages have variable rates linked to Euribor, the rate at which European banks lend to each other, plus a fixed spread.

P.title: mo-banks.c8.text
Money: Instant transfers, MB WAY and cards move money in seconds. Behind the scenes, banks settle with each other through central bank systems.

P.title: mo-banks.c9.text
Money: The ECB is preparing a possible digital euro, a central bank currency for everyday digital payments, alongside cash.

P.title: mo-retire.q0.q
Money: Who pays for current pensions in a pay-as-you-go system?

P.title: mo-retire.q1.q
Money: What is a PPR in Portugal?

P.title: mo-retire.q1.o1
Money: A retirement savings plan with tax benefits

P.title: mo-retire.q1.o2
Money: A pension paid by the state

P.title: mo-retire.c0.text
Money: Portugal's state pension is mostly pay-as-you-go: today's workers' contributions pay today's retirees. It depends on the ratio of workers to pensioners.

P.title: mo-retire.c1.text
Money: As people live longer and have fewer children, there are fewer workers per pensioner, putting pressure on pension systems.

P.title: mo-retire.c2.text
Money: Portugal links the retirement age to life expectancy: as people live longer, the statutory age rises gradually, now above 66.

P.title: mo-retire.c3.text
Money: The replacement rate is your pension as a share of your last salary. Projections suggest future retirees in Portugal may receive a lower share than today's.

P.title: mo-retire.c4.text
Money: Retirement income often rests on three pillars: the state pension, workplace pensions and personal savings.

P.title: mo-retire.c5.text
Money: Thanks to compounding, money saved in your 20s and 30s has decades to grow. Saving €100 a month from 25 can beat €200 a month from 45.

P.title: mo-retire.c6.text
Money: In Portugal, the Plano Poupança Reforma (PPR) is a retirement savings product with tax benefits on contributions, within limits, and rules on when you can withdraw.

P.title: mo-retire.c6.viz.items.1
Money: Withdrawal at retirement age or special cases

P.title: mo-retire.c7.text
Money: A rough guideline from US studies: withdrawing about 4% of a diversified portfolio in the first year, then adjusting for inflation, has historically lasted about 30 years. It's not a guarantee.

P.title: mo-retire.c8.text
Money: Over 25 years of retirement, 2% inflation reduces the buying power of a fixed pension by about 40%. Income that adjusts with inflation is valuable.

P.title: mo-retire.c9.text
Money: In Portugal, the Segurança Social Direta website shows your contribution history and a pension simulation. Checking it early helps planning.

P.title: mo-housing.q0.q
Money: Early in a mortgage, payments mostly go to…

P.title: mo-housing.q1.q
Money: What happened to many variable-rate mortgages in 2022–23?

P.title: mo-housing.c0.text
Money: Buying builds ownership but ties up money and brings costs like taxes, maintenance and interest. Renting gives flexibility. The right answer depends on prices, rates and how long you'll stay.

P.title: mo-housing.c1.text
Money: Portuguese banks typically lend up to 90% of the property value for a primary home, so you'll need at least 10% plus costs. Bigger deposits often get better spreads.

P.title: mo-housing.c2.text
Money: Beyond the deposit, buyers pay transfer tax (IMT, with exemptions for some young and first-time buyers), stamp duty, registration, valuation and bank fees.

P.title: mo-housing.c3.text
Money: Each monthly payment covers interest plus a slice of the loan. Early on, most goes to interest; later, most goes to repaying the loan.

P.title: mo-housing.c4.text
Money: A €200,000 loan over 30 years at 4% costs about €955 a month. At 3%, about €843. Over 30 years, that 1-point difference adds up to about €40,000.

P.title: mo-housing.c5.text
Money: Variable rates follow Euribor: cheaper when rates fall, painful when they rise, as in 2022–23. Fixed or mixed rates give certainty at a price.

P.title: mo-housing.c6.text
Money: Before borrowing, check you could still pay if rates rose by 2–3 points. Many families in 2023 saw payments jump by hundreds of euros.

P.title: mo-housing.c7.text
Money: Paying extra reduces either the term or the monthly payment. Reducing the term usually saves more interest. Check fees for early repayment.

P.title: mo-housing.c8.text
Money: Housing in Portuguese cities has become expensive relative to local incomes. Compare the house price with yearly household income to judge affordability.

P.title: mo-housing.c8.viz.f
Money: price-to-income = home price ÷ yearly household income

P.title: mo-housing.c9.text
Money: Add up mortgage interest, IMI property tax, condominium fees, insurance and maintenance (often ~1% of value a year) before comparing with rent.

P.title: mo-crypto.summary
Money: What it is and what it isn't.

P.title: mo-crypto.q0.q
Money: What is the maximum number of bitcoins?

P.title: mo-crypto.q1.o1
Money: A token designed to track a currency

P.title: mo-crypto.c0.text
Money: Bitcoin, launched in 2009 by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, is a digital currency with no central bank. A shared public ledger, the blockchain, records all transactions.

P.title: mo-crypto.c1.text
Money: A blockchain is a chain of blocks of transactions, each linked to the last with cryptography. Changing an old block would mean redoing all the work after it.

P.title: mo-crypto.c2.text
Money: Bitcoin "miners" compete to solve a mathematical puzzle; the winner adds the next block and earns new bitcoins. This proof-of-work uses lots of electricity.

P.title: mo-crypto.c3.text
Money: Only 21 million bitcoins will ever exist. The reward for mining halves about every four years, the "halving".

P.title: mo-crypto.c4.text
Money: Crypto prices swing wildly. Bitcoin has fallen more than 70% several times. That makes it a poor short-term store of value for money you'll need.

P.title: mo-crypto.c5.text
Money: Stablecoins are crypto tokens designed to track a currency like the dollar, usually backed by reserves. Some collapsed when their backing failed.

P.title: mo-crypto.c6.text
Money: Crypto is popular with scammers: fake investment platforms, "pig butchering" romance scams and fake celebrity endorsements. Transactions are hard to reverse.

P.title: mo-crypto.c7.text
Money: If a platform holds your crypto, you rely on it staying solvent and honest. When FTX collapsed in 2022, customers lost access to billions.

P.title: mo-crypto.c8.text
Money: The EU's MiCA regulation, applying from 2024–25, sets rules for crypto providers and stablecoins, including licensing and consumer protections.

P.title: mo-crypto.c9.text
Money: A common rule of thumb: only invest what you could afford to lose entirely, use regulated platforms, enable two-factor authentication and ignore "guaranteed" returns. Not advice.

P.title: mo-behaviour.summary
Money: Why smart people make money mistakes.

P.title: mo-behaviour.q0.q
Money: Holding losing shares too long hoping to break even is called…

P.title: mo-behaviour.q1.q
Money: What do frequent traders usually earn compared with patient investors?

P.title: mo-behaviour.q2.q
Money: Automatic pension enrolment is an example of…

P.title: mo-behaviour.q2.x
Money: It works by changing the default.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c0.text
Money: We overvalue rewards now versus later. Most people prefer €100 today to €110 next week, yet prefer €110 in 53 weeks to €100 in 52. The delay is the same.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c1.text
Money: We treat money in separate mental "pots". Someone may keep savings at 2% while carrying a card balance at 18%, losing money on the difference.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c2.text
Money: Investors hate losses so much they hold losing shares too long, hoping to break even, and sell winners too early: the disposition effect.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c3.text
Money: When everyone's buying, it feels safe to join; when everyone's selling, panic spreads. Bubbles and crashes are partly herd behaviour.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c4.text
Money: Investors who trade most often tend to earn less, mostly due to costs and poor timing. A famous study found the most active traders underperformed by several points a year.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c5.text
Money: We assume recent trends will continue: after a good year, people pile in; after a crash, they flee, often at the worst time.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c6.text
Money: We value things more once we own them. Mugs given to students were "worth" about twice as much to them as to those asked to buy them.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c7.text
Money: Small changes in how choices are presented can help: automatic pension enrolment and "save more tomorrow" plans boost saving without forcing anyone.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c8.text
Money: Higher income is linked to greater happiness, with some studies showing gains continue at higher incomes. Spending on experiences, others and saving time tends to give more joy.

P.title: mo-behaviour.c9.text
Money: Set up automatic transfers on payday into savings and investments. You can't spend what you don't see, and you skip the willpower battle.

P.title: mo-history.q0.q
Money: How many escudos was one euro worth?

P.title: mo-history.c0.text
Money: In 1630s Holland, rare tulip bulbs reportedly sold for the price of a house before prices collapsed in 1637. Historians now think the mania was smaller than legend says.

P.title: mo-history.c1.text
Money: In 1720 shares in Britain's South Sea Company soared and crashed. Isaac Newton lost a fortune and supposedly said he could calculate the stars but not the madness of people.

P.title: mo-history.c2.text
Money: The US stock market crashed in October 1929, helping trigger the Great Depression. Bank failures and policy mistakes deepened it.

P.title: mo-history.c3.text
Money: When governments print money to cover debts, prices can explode. In Germany in 1923, prices doubled every few days; in Zimbabwe in 2008, faster still.

P.title: mo-history.c4.text
Money: In 1944, major economies tied their currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold. In 1971 the US ended gold convertibility, starting today's floating currencies.

P.title: mo-history.c5.text
Money: In the late 1990s, internet companies with no profits soared. The Nasdaq fell nearly 80% from 2000 to 2002. A few survivors became giants.

P.title: mo-history.c6.text
Money: Risky US mortgages were bundled into complex securities. When house prices fell, losses spread worldwide. Lehman Brothers collapsed in September 2008.

P.title: mo-history.c7.text
Money: In 2011, during the euro debt crisis, Portugal received a €78 billion rescue from the EU and IMF, with tough austerity conditions. It exited the programme in 2014.

P.title: mo-history.c8.text
Money: The euro launched in 1999 for banks and in 2002 as notes and coins. Portugal swapped escudos at 200.482 escudos per euro.

P.title: mo-history.c9.text
Money: Crises share patterns: cheap credit, rising prices, "this time is different" stories, then a sudden reversal. Diversification and humility protect you.

P.title: mo-business.q0.q
Money: A café has €6,000 fixed costs and earns €2 per coffee. Break-even is…

P.title: mo-business.q1.q
Money: Why can a profitable company run out of cash?

P.title: mo-business.q1.o1
Money: Customers pay late while bills are due

P.title: mo-business.c0.text
Money: Revenue is money coming in from sales. Subtract costs and you get profit. A company can have huge revenue and still lose money.

P.title: mo-business.c1.text
Money: Gross margin is what's left after the direct cost of goods. Net margin is what's left after everything, including salaries, rent, interest and tax.

P.title: mo-business.c2.text
Money: Fixed costs, like rent, stay the same whatever you sell; variable costs, like ingredients, rise with each sale. Selling more spreads fixed costs.

P.title: mo-business.c3.text
Money: The break-even point is where revenue covers all costs. A café with €6,000 monthly fixed costs and €2 profit per coffee must sell 3,000 coffees a month.

P.title: mo-business.c3.viz.f
Money: break-even = fixed costs ÷ margin per unit

P.title: mo-business.c4.text
Money: Profit isn't cash. A business can be profitable on paper but run out of cash if customers pay late. Many small firms fail for this reason.

P.title: mo-business.c5.text
Money: Companies earn in different ways: selling products, subscriptions, advertising, commissions or licensing.

P.title: mo-business.c6.text
Money: Bigger companies can produce each unit more cheaply: bulk buying, specialised machines and spreading fixed costs.

P.title: mo-business.c7.text
Money: Warren Buffett looks for "moats": advantages that protect profits, like brands, network effects, patents or switching costs.

P.title: mo-business.c8.text
Money: A company's market value is its share price times the number of shares. The price-to-earnings ratio compares price with profit per share.

P.title: mo-business.c8.viz.f
Money: P/E = share price ÷ earnings per share

P.title: mo-business.c9.text
Money: Cups and lemons cost €0.40 per glass; you sell at €1.50. Your stall costs €33 a day. You break even at 30 glasses; glass 31 is profit.

P.title: mo-insurance.summary
Money: Paying a little to avoid a disaster.

P.title: mo-insurance.q0.o1
Money: What you pay before insurance covers the rest

P.title: mo-insurance.q1.q
Money: Which insurance is compulsory for cars in Portugal?

P.title: mo-insurance.c0.text
Money: Insurance pools many people's small payments to cover the few who suffer big losses. Each pays a predictable premium instead of risking ruin.

P.title: mo-insurance.c1.text
Money: Insurance is most valuable for losses you couldn't absorb: your home, liability, health, income. For small losses, saving yourself is often cheaper.

P.title: mo-insurance.c2.text
Money: The premium is what you pay regularly. The deductible (franquia) is what you pay before insurance kicks in. A higher deductible usually means a lower premium.

P.title: mo-insurance.c3.text
Money: In Portugal, car third-party liability insurance is compulsory. Fire insurance is required for buildings under horizontal property, and banks require it with mortgages.

P.title: mo-insurance.c3.viz.items.2
Money: Mortgage: life and multi-risk usually required

P.title: mo-insurance.c4.text
Money: Life insurance pays dependants if you die. It matters most when others rely on your income, like children or a partner with a shared mortgage.

P.title: mo-insurance.c5.text
Money: Portugal's SNS provides public healthcare. Private health insurance can cut waiting times for consultations, but check exclusions, caps and waiting periods.

P.title: mo-insurance.c6.text
Money: What's not covered matters as much as what is. Floods, earthquakes and pre-existing conditions are common exclusions.

P.title: mo-insurance.c7.text
Money: Once insured, people may take more risks, knowing someone else pays. Deductibles and co-payments help counter it.

P.title: mo-insurance.c8.text
Money: Given the 1755 history, earthquake cover in Portugal is optional and often excluded from standard home policies. Many homes are uninsured for it.

P.title: mo-insurance.c8.viz.items.0.r
Money: Check: it's often an optional extra

P.title: mo-insurance.c9.text
Money: Compare policies by cover, exclusions and deductible, not just premium. Review yearly; loyalty is rarely rewarded.

P.title: mo-scams.q0.q
Money: Will a real bank ask for your one-time SMS code?

P.title: mo-scams.q0.x
Money: Hang up and call the official number.

P.title: mo-scams.q1.q
Money: Where can you check if an investment company is authorised in Portugal?

P.title: mo-scams.q1.o1
Money: CMVM and Banco de Portugal lists

P.title: mo-scams.c0.text
Money: Most scams create urgency: "your account will be blocked", "act now". Pressure stops you thinking. Real banks don't rush you like that.

P.title: mo-scams.c1.text
Money: Fake emails, SMS or calls pretend to be your bank, the tax authority or a delivery company, asking you to click a link or share codes.

P.title: mo-scams.c2.text
Money: No real bank will ask for your full card PIN, online banking password or the one-time code sent to your phone. Anyone asking is a scammer.

P.title: mo-scams.c2.viz.items.0.w
Money: The bank called asking for my code

P.title: mo-scams.c2.viz.items.0.r
Money: Hang up, call the bank's official number

P.title: mo-scams.c3.text
Money: Scammers message parents claiming to be their child with a new number, asking urgently for money. Call the child's old number to check.

P.title: mo-scams.c4.text
Money: Fake platforms show impressive returns and let you withdraw small amounts to build trust, then disappear with larger deposits. Check regulators' warning lists.

P.title: mo-scams.c5.text
Money: In Portugal, the CMVM, Banco de Portugal and ASF publish lists of unauthorised entities. If a company isn't registered, don't invest.

P.title: mo-scams.c6.text
Money: Scammers build online relationships over weeks, then invent emergencies or investment "opportunities". Never send money to someone you haven't met.

P.title: mo-scams.c7.text
Money: Use contactless and app notifications, set spending limits and use virtual cards for online shopping. Report a lost card immediately.

P.title: mo-scams.c8.text
Money: Scammers posing as buyers on marketplaces ask you to "receive" money via MB WAY but actually guide you to send it or link their phone to your account.

P.title: mo-scams.c8.viz.items.0.w
Money: Go to the ATM to receive payment

P.title: mo-scams.c8.viz.items.0.r
Money: Receiving money never requires you to act at an ATM

P.title: mo-scams.c9.text
Money: Contact your bank immediately to block cards and transfers, change passwords, report to the police and keep evidence. Speed improves the odds of recovery.

P.title: mo-markets.q0.o1
Money: A fall of 20% or more from a peak

P.title: mo-markets.q0.x
Money: Bulls charge up; bears swipe down.

P.title: mo-markets.q1.o1
Money: A basket of assets traded like a share

P.title: mo-markets.q2.q
Money: What is Portugal's main stock index?

P.title: mo-markets.c0.text
Money: Companies sell shares on a stock exchange to raise money for growth. Early investors can also sell their stakes. Listing for the first time is an IPO.

P.title: mo-markets.c1.text
Money: Stock exchanges are marketplaces matching buyers and sellers. Portugal's is Euronext Lisbon; its main index, the PSI, tracks the largest listed companies.

P.title: mo-markets.c2.text
Money: Prices move with supply and demand, driven by expected future profits, interest rates, news and sentiment.

P.title: mo-markets.c3.text
Money: An index tracks a basket of shares to show how a market is doing. The S&P 500 includes about 500 of the largest US companies, weighted by size.

P.title: mo-markets.c4.text
Money: A bull market is a sustained rise; a bear market is a fall of 20% or more from a peak. Bulls charge up; bears swipe down.

P.title: mo-markets.c5.text
Money: Over long periods, global shares have returned roughly 5% a year above inflation on average, but with big swings and some long flat periods.

P.title: mo-markets.c6.text
Money: Even good markets have big falls. World shares fell about 50% in 2008–09 and around 34% in weeks in early 2020, then recovered.

P.title: mo-markets.c7.text
Money: Exchange-traded funds hold baskets of assets and trade like shares. A single world ETF can give you thousands of companies at low cost.

P.title: mo-markets.c8.text
Money: Fund fees (TER), trading commissions, currency conversion and taxes all eat into returns. Over decades, small differences compound.

P.title: mo-markets.c9.text
Money: Gains from selling shares and dividends are generally taxed at a flat 28% in Portugal, with the option to include them in income tax. Rules change; check current law.

P.title: mo-trade.q1.q
Money: Since when has the EU single market existed?

P.title: mo-trade.q1.x
Money: Free movement of goods, services, people and capital.

P.title: mo-trade.c0.text
Money: Trade lets countries specialise and consumers enjoy cheaper, more varied goods. Portugal exports cars, machinery, cork, wine, clothing and tourism services.

P.title: mo-trade.c1.text
Money: Tourism is one of Portugal's biggest export earners, bringing in tens of millions of visitors a year, about three times the population.

P.title: mo-trade.c2.text
Money: A country with a trade deficit imports more than it exports. It's not automatically bad: it may be investing or consuming with foreign financing.

P.title: mo-trade.c3.text
Money: A tariff is a tax on imports. It protects some domestic producers but raises prices for consumers and can trigger retaliation.

P.title: mo-trade.c4.text
Money: Since 1993, goods, services, people and capital move freely across EU member states, the world's largest single market by many measures.

P.title: mo-trade.c5.text
Money: Products cross many borders before you buy them. The pandemic and the 2021 Suez Canal blockage showed how fragile long supply chains can be.

P.title: mo-trade.c6.text
Money: Commodities like oil, wheat, coffee and copper are traded globally. Their prices affect inflation, fuel bills and food prices everywhere.

P.title: mo-trade.c7.text
Money: When the US Federal Reserve or the ECB raises rates, borrowing gets more expensive across the world, affecting currencies, mortgages and markets.

P.title: mo-trade.c8.text
Money: Fast-growing economies like India, Indonesia and Brazil are a growing share of world output. China became the world's largest economy by purchasing power around 2016.

P.title: mo-trade.c9.text
Money: Migrants send money home: remittances to low- and middle-income countries exceed $650 billion a year, more than foreign aid.

P.title: mo-negotiate.q0.o1
Money: Your best alternative if the deal fails

P.title: mo-negotiate.q1.q
Money: What should you compare between job offers?

P.title: mo-negotiate.q1.o1
Money: Net pay and the total package

P.title: mo-negotiate.c0.text
Money: Research typical pay for your role, experience and location from job sites, industry surveys and peers. Data beats feelings in negotiation.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c1.text
Money: Your BATNA is your best alternative to a negotiated agreement: what you'll do if this deal fails. The stronger it is, the stronger your position.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c2.text
Money: The first number tends to anchor the discussion. If you have good data, naming an ambitious but justified number first can work in your favour.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c3.text
Money: Salary isn't everything: bonus, meal allowance, health insurance, remote work, training budget and holidays all have value.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c4.text
Money: The best times to ask are after a big success, during performance reviews or when taking on new responsibilities. Bring evidence of impact.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c5.text
Money: Ask what the other side needs: budget limits, timing, priorities. Creative solutions often satisfy both, like a later start date for a higher salary.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c6.text
Money: After making an offer or receiving one, pause. People often fill silence with concessions.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c7.text
Money: In Portugal, the gap between gross and net pay includes social security (11% for employees) and IRS withholding. Compare offers in net terms.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c8.text
Money: A €2,000 difference in starting salary, compounded through raises over a career, can add up to tens of thousands of euros.

P.title: mo-negotiate.c9.text
Money: I'm excited about this role. Based on my research and experience in X, I was expecting something closer to €Y. Is there flexibility?

P.title: mo-goals.q1.q
Money: Where should money needed in two years usually be kept?

P.title: mo-goals.c0.text
Money: Vague goals ("save more") rarely work. Make them specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound: "save €6,000 for a car by December 2027".

P.title: mo-goals.c1.text
Money: Your net worth is what you own minus what you owe. Tracking it once or twice a year shows if you're moving forward.

P.title: mo-goals.c2.text
Money: A common sequence: build a small buffer, clear expensive debt, build a full emergency fund, then save for goals and invest for the long term.

P.title: mo-goals.c3.text
Money: Money needed within 2–3 years belongs in safe places. Money for 10+ years can tolerate the ups and downs of investing.

P.title: mo-goals.c4.text
Money: Save monthly for known irregular costs, like car insurance, holidays or Christmas, so they don't become emergencies.

P.title: mo-goals.c5.text
Money: Your savings rate, the share of income you save, matters more than investment returns early on. Going from 5% to 15% has a huge effect over time.

P.title: mo-goals.c6.text
Money: Once a year, review income, spending, debts, insurance, investments and goals. Life changes; your plan should too.

P.title: mo-goals.c7.text
Money: Money is a top cause of conflict. Talk openly about goals and habits; many couples use a shared account for joint costs plus personal accounts.

P.title: mo-goals.c8.text
Money: Pocket money, saving jars and letting children make small mistakes teach money skills early. Habits form by age 7, some research suggests.

P.title: mo-goals.c9.text
Money: On one page: monthly income, fixed costs, savings rate, emergency fund target, debts with rates and two or three goals with dates.

P.title: mo-tax.q0.q
Money: In a progressive system, a raise into a higher bracket means…

P.title: mo-tax.q0.o1
Money: only the extra income is taxed more

P.title: mo-tax.q1.q
Money: What is the standard IVA rate in mainland Portugal?

P.title: mo-tax.c0.text
Money: Taxes fund public services: healthcare, schools, roads, pensions and defence. In Portugal, taxes and social contributions are roughly 35–38% of GDP.

P.title: mo-tax.c1.text
Money: Direct taxes are on income and wealth, like IRS. Indirect taxes are on spending, like IVA and fuel taxes, and are paid by everyone who buys.

P.title: mo-tax.c2.text
Money: IRS is progressive: higher slices of income are taxed at higher rates. Only the income within each bracket pays that bracket's rate.

P.title: mo-tax.c3.text
Money: Moving into a higher bracket never reduces your take-home pay overall: only the extra income is taxed at the higher rate. Your average rate is always lower than your top rate.

P.title: mo-tax.c3.viz.items.0.w
Money: A raise pushed me into a higher bracket, so I earn less

P.title: mo-tax.c3.viz.items.0.r
Money: Only the extra euros are taxed more

P.title: mo-tax.c4.text
Money: Portugal's mainland IVA has three rates: 6% for essentials like basic food, 13% for some items like restaurant food, and 23% standard. The islands have lower rates.

P.title: mo-tax.c5.text
Money: Asking for an invoice with your NIF lets some spending count for IRS deductions, like health, education and housing, and helps fight tax evasion.

P.title: mo-tax.c6.text
Money: Deductions reduce the tax you owe: health, education, rent and dependants are common categories, each with limits.

P.title: mo-tax.c7.text
Money: Portugal offers reduced income tax for young workers in their first years of work, under the IRS Jovem scheme. The rules have changed several times; check current conditions.

P.title: mo-tax.c8.text
Money: Self-employed workers issue "recibos verdes", pay social security quarterly declarations and may use a simplified regime where only part of income is taxed.

P.title: mo-tax.c9.text
Money: Each spring, check the pre-filled IRS on the Portal das Finanças. Confirm dependants, deductions and income before submitting; automatic IRS suits many.
